See how this bachelor compares with study options at UCR

This is a pre-produced programme comparison. Your search helped you find the programme; it did not personalize the comparison.

← Back to search

VU Criminology examines offending, victims, criminalization and society’s responses through criminological theory, law, psychology, sociology and empirical research. Its Dutch-language degree includes a group investigation with an individual thesis and an open minor period.

UCR offers one qualified interdisciplinary approach through criminal accountability, social and developmental psychology, mental disorder, sociological explanation and empirical methods. Youth resilience to radicalization supplies a specific prevention contribution; media courses study representation. These are substantive related contributions, but they do not reproduce VU’s specialist criminological theory, crime measurement, criminal procedure, victimology, penology or supervised thesis. General clinical psychology does not establish forensic expertise, and international law does not teach domestic criminal procedure. This curriculum does not establish professional qualification or automatic admission to a master’s programme.

Academic year: 2026–2027

The Dutch-language 2026–2027 degree contains 180 EC: ten compulsory 6 EC units in each of Years 1 and 2; four compulsory Year-3 units totaling 30 EC, including the 12 EC research-skills unit; and 30 EC of open study. The research unit combines group investigation with an individual thesis. Entry requires both quantitative and qualitative criminological methods to be passed; registration for periods 5–6 uses the VU dashboard and regular deadlines, with instructions on Canvas. Principles of Criminal Law precedes substantive and procedural criminal law. Open study requires prior board approval except qualifying university or listed minors; individual coherent packages and exchange allow at most 6 EC at level 100 and require at least 12 EC at level 300. A minor must be completed in full. Internships cannot replace minor credit and may carry at most 6 extracurricular EC. The optional Forensic Criminology minor is not a compulsory route. The diagnostic Dutch test and any required remedial course must be passed for the first-year criminology project grade. Professional and personal identity coaching runs alongside credited units. Practical/tutorial attendance applies unless the course instructions specify otherwise. The ordinary first-year study-advice threshold is 42 EC. Noncredit obligations, optional honours and earlier-cohort transitions add no credits to this pathway.

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Research Methods & Statistics
Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, sampling, experiments and surveys. Students study descriptive and inferential statistics, association, hypothesis testing and analysis of variance, with an introduction to multivariate applications. A group research project applies these methods to a chosen research problem.
Close

Introduction to Data Science
Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students explore legal systems and fields including constitutional, administrative, criminal and international law, human rights and selected private-law topics. Case law and trial simulations support discussion of law, society and justice.
Close

Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
Close

Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduction to Public International Law examines the creation and historical development of international law, its sources, subjects and organisation. Topics include the use of force, armed conflict, international criminal law, refugees and environmental law, followed by self-determination, Third World Approaches and treaty politics. Assessment includes exercises, exams, a podcast and reflection.
Close

Ethics
Ethics examines virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism, alongside moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Students apply ethical arguments to issues including equality, poverty and wealth, animal rights, future generations, climate change and historical injustice. Papers and presentations develop independent argumentation.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential Western thinkers from classical antiquity to the present. Students study views of human nature, society and political authority, place theories in their historical settings and compare their arguments and proposed solutions with contemporary political problems.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Peace & Conflict introduces theories about the causes, consequences and possible resolution of violent and nonviolent conflicts. Historical and contemporary cases address structural inequality, ideology, humiliation and colonial or postcolonial grievances. Students compare international, institutional, cultural and civil-society perspectives and examine how concepts such as justice, truth and reconciliation travel between fields.
Close

Introduction to Sociology
Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

Modern Sociology
Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

Introduction to Brain & Behavior
Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
Close

Social Psychology
Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
Close

Statistics & Experimental Methods
Teaches multivariate statistical methods for research on complex human phenomena. Topics include linear and logistic regression, factor analysis, analysis of variance and covariance, and non-parametric tests. Students select and apply models, assess statistical problems and report their analyses.
Close

Abnormal Psychology
Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.
Close

Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies
Introduces concepts, methods and ethical issues in clinical psychological assessment and psychotherapy. Students compare approaches to assessment and treatment across age groups and learn to evaluate information critically.
Close

Advanced Research Seminar
Advanced Research Seminar introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.
Close

Lifespan Developmental Psychology
Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
Close

Youth Resilience to Extremism
Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
Close

Media & Race
Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
Close

The Documentary
Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
Close
